open_points.subject: Syncthing evidence topology
open_points.question: Were the two instances connected peers exercising real synchronization, independent instances tested separately, or another topology, and where were they hosted?
options: Two peered instances synchronized files end to end
Two independent instances were exercised separately
One or both instances were only API or filesystem test fixtures
open_points.default_guess: Treat them as two peered, locally hosted real Syncthing processes.

witness.initial: A chosen photo exists only in a folder served by the first Syncthing instance.
events: The first instance advertises the folder to the second instance.
The delivery flow reads the photo from the second instance.
outcomes: The evidence claim covers propagation between two real peers before delivery.
The evidence claim only means each instance was contacted separately and does not cover propagation.
witness.observer: A reviewer deciding whether synchronization behavior has been exercised

open_points.subject: Syncthing action coverage
open_points.text: and against two private Syncthing instances
open_points.question: Which primary actions, failures, and observable results were exercised against the Syncthing instances?
options: Only connection and folder availability were exercised
Connection, listing, delivery and repeat delivery were exercised
Every applicable success and failure in the table was exercised
open_points.default_guess: Assume connection, listing and delivery success paths were exercised, but no failure path unless stated.

witness.initial: A confirmed project connection points to a synchronized photo folder.
events: The owner asks to see deliverable files.
The calling flow chooses and delivers one photo.
The same photo is delivered again.
outcomes: All three operations were run with the real Syncthing instances.
Only folder connection was run with Syncthing; the later operations used fixtures.
witness.observer: A reviewer relying on the evidence column

open_points.subject: Relationship between Portal and Syncthing runs
open_points.text: Evidence is from local runs against a real Client Portal process with a stub Registry, and against two private Syncthing instances.
open_points.question: Did a single end-to-end run use the real Portal process, stub Registry and Syncthing instances together, or were these separate runs?
options: One integrated end-to-end run used all named systems
Portal/Registry and Syncthing were exercised in separate runs
Both integrated and separate runs were performed
open_points.default_guess: Assume they were separate runs because integration is not stated.

witness.initial: A synchronized source photo is ready for delivery and no Portal photo exists.
events: The delivery flow prepares and places the image.
The calling flow publishes it through the Portal.
outcomes: One run crossed Syncthing, the stub Registry and the real Portal.
Separate runs tested each boundary, so their combined behavior remains untested.

open_points.subject: Private Syncthing trust boundary
open_points.question: Who controlled and could access these instances, and did they represent separate device or user trust boundaries?
options: Both instances were controlled by the implementer on one machine
The instances ran on separate private machines under one owner
The instances belonged to different actors or security domains
open_points.default_guess: Assume both were implementer-controlled local instances and did not exercise an owner-device trust boundary.

open_points.subject: Excluded deployment components
open_points.text: the owner's devices, the kernel or the VPS
open_points.question: What exact devices, component called “the kernel,” and VPS deployment are excluded, and which promised actions or interfaces depend on each?
options: “kernel” means the operating-system kernel and device filesystem behavior
“kernel” is a product service or component
The phrase denotes the complete production deployment path
open_points.default_guess: Treat these as three untested production boundaries: owner hardware, a product component named kernel, and VPS hosting.
